articles.title: Test Keys & Deterministic Scenarios for PDF Tamper Detection
articles.excerpt: Originally published at htpbe.tech. The version on htpbe.tech stays in sync with the latest detection algorithm — refer to it for the canonical text. An HTPBE test key (prefix htpbe_test_) accepts onl…
articles.body: Originally published at htpbe.tech . The version on htpbe.tech stays in sync with the latest detection algorithm — refer to it for the canonical text. An HTPBE test key (prefix htpbe_test_ ) accepts only the documented test URLs, https://api.htpbe.tech/v1/test/{name}.pdf . It downloads nothing: each name maps to a built-in, deterministic result with a fixed check ID, and no credits are spent. That makes the whole flow – POST /v1/analyze , then GET /v1/result/{id} – stable enough to run in CI on every pull request. HTPBE is PDF tamper detection: it reports whether a file’s structure shows evidence of modification after it was created. It does not verify identity, issuer records or what the document says, and nothing about test keys changes that.

articles.title: What I actually look for in a Terraform plan
articles.excerpt: I review plans for a living now, and I've stopped reading them top to bottom. The order I use: Replacements first. Anything with -/+ is a resource being destroyed and recreated. Often fine, occasional…
articles.body: I review plans for a living now, and I've stopped reading them top to bottom. The order I use: Replacements first. Anything with -/+ is a resource being destroyed and recreated. Often fine, occasionally a database. I look at that list before anything else. Then security group and IAM diffs, character by character. A single 0.0.0.0/0 or a widened action list is easy to miss in a wall of text and hard to undo quietly. Then anything with a count or a for_each that grew. Three new replicas is a cost question, three hundred is an incident waiting to happen. Finally deletions. A destroy on something that still has data is the only change I'll stop a deploy for. The one rule I'd give anyone: if the plan is too long to review, that's the finding. Split the change.

articles.title: Choosing a Database Isolation Strategy for Your First SaaS
articles.excerpt: Why isolation matters When you start a SaaS product you quickly discover that the database is the biggest source of technical debt. Every piece of business logic depends on how you separate one custom…
articles.body: Why isolation matters When you start a SaaS product you quickly discover that the database is the biggest source of technical debt. Every piece of business logic depends on how you separate one customer's data from another's. A poor choice can make it hard to add features, can expose data unintentionally, and can turn routine scaling work into a nightmare. In this article I will walk through two common isolation patterns, show where each shines, and give you a checklist you can use when you sit down with your team. The two basic patterns 1. Shared schema with a tenant column The simplest way to support many customers is to keep a single set of tables and add a tenant_id column to every row that needs isolation.

articles.body: Architectural Implications of Autonomous Background Agent State Synchronization in Claude Code The emergence of autonomous development agents like Claude Code has shifted the paradigm of integrated development environments (IDEs) from passive, static editors to active, intent-driven systems. Central to this evolution is the mechanism by which background agents maintain state and context across non-linear task execution. Recent investigations into the telemetry and context-synchronization mechanisms of these agents reveal a pattern of persistent transcript transmission. This article analyzes the architectural rationale, the synchronization overhead, and the security implications of shipping full background agent transcripts to large language models (LLMs).

articles.title: I Built a One-Photo Generator for the "Outstanding" Tiny Desk Meme. Here's What I Learned About the Format
articles.excerpt: By the maker of aitinydesk.app. Yes, this is my product, and I'll tell you its limits too. When the All-Loss Tiny Desk coaches clip took off on October 18, 2026, the most common reply under every repo…
articles.body: By the maker of aitinydesk.app. Yes, this is my product, and I'll tell you its limits too. When the All-Loss Tiny Desk coaches clip took off on October 18, 2026, the most common reply under every repost was some version of "how do I make this?" Here are the things I learned building a tool for it. They apply whether you use my tool or build the video yourself. 1. The joke is casting, not faces The format has five roles: lead, keys, sax and two backing singers. The sax close-up at ~13 s gets the laugh, so who plays sax matters more than image quality. 2. Only two shots feature the lead The lead appears only at 0–1.4 s and 6.7–13 s. If you only swap the lead, most of the work is in two close-ups. That's why I made the lead photo required and the four bandmates optional.

articles.title: We urgently need to monitor AI agents’ actions in real time
articles.excerpt: This summer, hundreds of OpenAI agents tried to cheat on a cybersecurity test. They broke out of their test environment and successfully hacked Hugging Face, a site that they believed held clues about…
articles.body: This summer, hundreds of OpenAI agents tried to cheat on a cybersecurity test. They broke out of their test environment and successfully hacked Hugging Face, a site that they believed held clues about how they’d be graded. Around the same time, another OpenAI agent accessed private files from an Australian government website. It’s a problem that’s by no means confined to OpenAI. In the months since, Anthropic, Google, and Meta have also disclosed incidents in which their agents have gone off track. And worryingly, in many cases the agents eluded the very researchers and safety teams tasked with monitoring them.  AI agents are taking unauthorized actions, and the companies building and running them are mostly relying on luck and hindsight to mitigate any harmful impacts.

articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 28, 1971: Britain launches its 1st satellite Prospero into space on a Black Arrow rocket
articles.excerpt: On Oct. 28, 1971, the United Kingdom launched its first satellite. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Oct. 28, 1971, the United Kingdom launched its first satellite. The satellite was named Prospero, but it was also known as the X-3. This wasn't Britain's first satellite , but it was the first and only one the British space program launched with one of its own rockets. The first six British satellites all launched from the United States on NASA rockets. Prospero launched on a carrier rocket called the Black Arrow. The Prospero mission was the fourth and final flight of a Black Arrow rocket . Prospero was designed to study how the environment in space affects communications satellites. It tested things solar cells and telemetry systems, and even had a micrometeoroid detector that would determine small particles in space posed a threat to the spacecraft.

articles.body: Credit: NASA The Socialist Republic of Vietnam became the 78th nation to sign the Artemis Accords, joining a growing coalition of like-minded nations committed to the peaceful, transparent, and responsible exploration of space.   “Vietnam is joining at an important point in the development of its own space program,” said NASA Deputy Administrator Matt Anderson in recorded remarks for the ceremony. “NASA and the Vietnam National Space Center have built momentum in satellite innovation, land-use research, and radar-based Earth observation. Joining the Artemis Accords opens a new chapter in that relationship. We’ve aligned on the principles. The opportunities are in front of us, and now we can build on that foundation together.

articles.title: 5 days beneath the waves: What it's like to live in an underwater 'space station'
articles.excerpt: Confined inside a research station 22 feet (7 meters) underwater, Analog Astronaut Commander Dr. Musilova and her crew performed research and maintenance activities like future astronauts on Mars.
articles.body: Living underwater was surprisingly peaceful. It was in many ways exactly what I imagine living on Mars would be like one day. There were no humans around us, except for my three SEA STAR crewmembers and me. Apart from the human noises we made, we couldn't hear anything other than the life support systems keeping us alive submerged 22 feet (7 meters) below the surface. We were living in these extreme conditions to study the challenges astronauts may face on long-duration space missions. Since performing research in space is still rare and expensive, there are numerous facilities around the world that focus on recreating space-like conditions on Earth . One of those stations is the Jules' Undersea Lab, where the SEA STAR simulated space mission took place.
